title: Release Audits Are the Missing Spec
stat: 74 percent of platform teams now run an automated step inside release, up from 41 percent two years ago
source: A cross-industry survey of platform engineering leads
topic_claim: the practice of treating release logs as settled is now the default answer
story_examples: One release sheet listed forty changes and named owners for none of them.
Another team merged six fixes into one deploy and wrote a single ticket line for all of them.
A third rebuilt the same report twice because nobody recorded which version shipped.
thesis: Every fix costs more than it should because nothing tracks which change a correction touched. Release audits cost less than the rework they prevent. The audit trail is where that cost gets paid, one line at a time
design_moves: require the ticket link next to every fixed line
review the log instead of the document
counter: the fixed-review story no longer matches what automated pipelines and their silent defaults actually ship
definition: Release audit is the work a reviewer must spend to trace a shipped change back to its ticket
gap_stat_a: 68 percent of teams say traceability decides their trust in a release
gap_stat_b: only 22 percent can show where a correction landed
takeaway: Write the log you would want run on you: expose the ticket, log the cut, show the diff.
question_tail: Which step in your release process still claims a record it cannot show?
person_context: I maintain a release pipeline for a platform team
